The case investigation form includes data elements such as demographic information, clinical findings, neonatal outcomes, maternal and perinatal risk factors, and public health response efforts. 2. Data analysis involves calculating the number and incidence of confirmed cases per 1,000 live births, categorized by month, year, sex, and district. 3. The percentage of confirmed cases that were protected at birth (PAB) due to maternal vaccination is assessed. 4. The percentage of confirmed cases whose mothers received antenatal care (ANC) is analyzed. 5. Among mothers who received ANC, the percentage of those who were not vaccinated is evaluated to identify missed opportunities for immunization. 6. The percentage of confirmed cases is categorized by the place of birth (health facility or home delivery), type of birth assistance, type of cord-cutting tools used, and type of umbilical cord dressing applied. 7. Maternal factors such as age and parity (first birth or multiple births) are considered in the analysis. 8. The distribution of outcomes among confirmed cases, including death, leaving against medical advice, survival, or unknown outcomes, is documented. 9. The case fatality ratio among confirmed cases is calculated. 10. The percentage of confirmed cases whose mothers received a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) dose after the case occurred, as a result of case detection or investigation, is determined. 11. The percentage of neonatal deaths attributable to neonatal tetanus (NT), if part of neonatal death surveillance, is calculated. 12. The percentage of confirmed cases that triggered an active search in the community is assessed. 13. The percentage of confirmed cases that led to an immunization response among women of reproductive age is evaluated. 14. Surveillance data should be triangulated with immunization program data, such as vaccination coverage, supplementary immunization activities (SIAs), ANC coverage, and skilled birth attendance (SBA) coverage, to provide a comprehensive understanding for policy and strategy formulation. 15. Surveillance data can be used to monitor the achievement and maintenance of maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination (MNTE), defined as less than one NT case per 1,000 live births in every district. 16. Data may be incorporated into annual risk assessments to identify high-risk geographical areas for targeted improvements in antenatal, obstetric, and vaccination services, as well as targeted SIAs for women of reproductive age. 17. Surveillance data can help identify NT risk factors, such as place and type of delivery, cord care practices, maternal age and parity, and migrant or ethnic status, to design appropriate messaging and interventions. 18. The impact of interventions, including SIAs, can be monitored using surveillance data. 19. Missed opportunities for maternal immunization with TTCV can be identified through data analysis. 20. Evidence from surveillance data may inform changes in immunization policy or strategy, such as introducing WHO-recommended booster doses or school-based immunization programs if first-time mothers are not being reached during ANC visits. 21. Surveillance data can facilitate the rapid identification of cases for appropriate case management. 22. Countries should annually review the performance of each district in a joint exercise involving the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), maternal, neonatal, and child health (MNCH) programs, surveillance managers, and partner representatives. 23. Districts should be classified as low risk or at risk for MNTE, with further classification of at risk districts into high risk and medium risk to tailor corrective strategies effectively. 24. Ethical and equity considerations must be addressed during surveillance, as neonatal deaths are sensitive topics, particularly among marginalized groups such as migrants, the homeless, and urban slum residents. 25. Serological surveys of tetanus IgG among adult women may complement monitoring of MNTE risk and guide vaccination strategies, as tetanus immunity reflects vaccination coverage rather than natural infection. 26. Serosurveillance should not replace NT surveillance but should be carefully designed to ensure valid and interpretable results. 27. Tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, whose spores are present in soil contaminated with animal and human feces. The spores enter the body through skin breaks and germinate under anaerobic conditions, producing the toxin tetanospasmin, which causes painful muscular contractions. 28. Neonatal tetanus typically results from unhygienic delivery practices, such as using non-sterile instruments to cut the umbilical cord or applying contaminated materials to the umbilical stump. 29. The incubation period for neonatal tetanus is usually 3 to 14 days, averaging 7 days, with shorter periods associated with more severe disease and worse prognosis. 30. The disease is not directly transmitted from person to person, and the case fatality ratio is exceedingly high, exceeding 80% in cases with a short incubation period and low birth weight. 31. The tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine, available as a single-antigen vaccine or in combination with vaccines against diphtheria, pertussis, poliomyelitis, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). 32. The pentavalent vaccine (DTP-Hib-HepB) is the most commonly used childhood vaccine worldwide to prevent NT, but other pentavalent and hexavalent combinations are also available. 33. Booster doses of tetanus-diphtheria combination vaccines with lower diphtheria antigen concentrations are recommended, and single-antigen vaccines should be discontinued when feasible to maintain high immunity levels throughout life. 34. The effectiveness of at least two properly timed doses of TTCV given to pregnant women or women of reproductive age against NT mortality is 94% (95% CI: 80–98%). 35. Despite the availability of effective TTCV vaccines, tetanus continues to have a significant global health impact, with an estimated 25,000 neonatal deaths in 2018, representing an 88% reduction from 200,000 deaths in 2000. 36. Approximately 47 million women and their infants remain unprotected against tetanus, highlighting the need for continued efforts to address this gap. 37. Timeliness of investigation is critical, with a target of investigating at least 80% of suspected cases within 7 days of notification. 38. Adequacy of investigation is defined as having complete information on all core variables for at least 80% of suspected cases. 39. Core variables include case identification, date of birth, sex, place of residence, date of illness onset, date of notification, date of investigation, symptoms, outcome, maternal vaccination history, place/type of delivery, cord-cutting tool, and material applied to the cord. 40. Maintenance of MNTE requires that 100% of districts report less than one NT case per 1,000 live births. 41. Adequate case response involves ensuring that 100% of mothers of NT cases receive a TTCV dose in conjunction with case detection or investigation. 42. Surveillance systems must be sensitive and effective to detect and investigate every NT case, ensuring appropriate remedial measures are implemented.
